To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ionisation degree can have different chemical life cycles in different layers of the disc, that the chemistry of the midplane is driven by the decay of radionuclidic elements, that surface reactions are important in the intermediate layer and that the surface layer can be accurately described in terms of photoionisation and recombination.

the ionization degree in the dead zone of a protoplanetary disc is very low, it is sustained only by radionuclde decay and cosmic rays, and its chemistry can be accurately reproduced in reduced chemical networks containing about 10 key species and a similar number reactions.
the evolution of the chemical composition in a protoplanetary disc can be reduced by several orders of magnitude without losing accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reduction of chemical networks in protoplanetary disc modelling.
the reduction of chemical models for protoplanetary discs to a manageable size, and with the identification of key reactions that govern the chemistry in different layers of the discs.
the reduction of chemical networks in protoplanetary disks and the analysis of the evolution of the chemical composition in the disc.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fractional ionisation degree in the disc is controlled by a very complex interplay of various physical and chemical processes, which can only be described by a large chemical network.
the chemistry of the ionisation fraction in protoplanetary disc is very rich.
the chemistry of protoplanetary disks is complex and that it is not yet possible to reduce the chemical networks to a small number of reactions and species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemistry of the ionisation is a very complicated problem, and that a reduction to a few key species is possible only in a few specific locations.

the ionisation degree can vary over many orders of magnitude in protoplanetary disc models, but the chemical networks required to reproduce the evolution of this quantity can be reduced significantly.
the chemistry of the ionisation in the disc can be described by reduced chemical models that can be easily coupled to MHD simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ionisation degree and chemistry in a protoplanetary disc can be reproduced by a small number of species and reactions, but the number of species and reaction steps required to reproduce the chemistry depends on the location in the disc.
a reduced set of chemical species and reactions is sufficient to accurately describe the fractional ionisation at all disc locations.
the chemistry of protoplanetary disc is highly complex and cannot be reduced to simple chemical networks.
